1489.etyen:
Borrowed from Latin āmēn (“amen; so be it”), from Koine Greek ᾱ̓μήν (āmḗn, “truly, certainly; so be it”), from Biblical Hebrew אָמֵן (“certainly, truly; amen”). The Hebrew word originally expressed truth or certainty and is related to a Hebrew verb meaning “to strengthen, confirm”. The word is already attested in Old Norwegian around 1200 in the Gammelnorsk homiliebok.
The noun is a nominalization of the interjection.

38353.etyen:

Compare Norwegian Nynorsk mil, Danish mil, Swedish mil, Icelandic míla, Faroese míla and English mile. / Unknown.

a surname originating as a patronymic, originally meaning “son of Svend”

1001937.etyen:
From Svend (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Svend”. The first element is Danish Svend m, the Danish form of Svein, ultimately from Old Norse Sveinn m, a personal name based on sveinn (“young man, servant”).
Compare the parallel Norwegian formation Svensen (“patronymic surname”), Danish Svendsen, Swedish Svensson and Icelandic Sveinsson (“patronymic surname”).

1002193.etyen:
From Old West Norse brattr, from Proto-Germanic *brantaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewsóm., of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰren- (“project”), related to Old English brant (“steep”), Latvian bruôds (“roof ridge”).
Cognate with Faroese and Icelandic brattur, Danish brat, Swedish brant, and Old English brant, bront (English brant, brent, Scots brent).

1004753.etyen:
From lever (“liver”) + kake (“cake, patty”), literally “liver cake”.
The first element lever (“liver”) continues lifr (“liver”), from *librō (“liver”); the second element kake (“cake, patty”) continues Old Norse kaka (“cake”).
Compare Swedish leverkaka (“liver cake”).

en.g: selection thinning; a thinning method in which dominant trees are felled in order to promote suppressed or subordinate trees
x: må ikke tas til inntekt for bledningstynning

1005009.etyen:
First attested in the by 1944.
Compound of bledning (“selection system”) + tynning (“thinning”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “selection-system thinning”. The first element is the verbal noun bledning (“selection system”) of dialectal ble (“to choose, select; select trees for felling”). The second element is the verbal noun of tynne (“to thin”), from Old Norse þynna (“to make thin”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þunnijaną (“to make thin”), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch”).
